::: {.lead}
Rana works in the *Sunrise* shop. Every evening she adds up the sales on a
calculator, and every week she makes a mistake. Excel can do the
calculation for her, and it does it again by itself when a number changes.
In lecture 5 you met Excel: a **workbook** with **worksheets** and
**cells**. In this lesson you make Excel calculate: you write **formulas**,
you copy them, and you use the first **functions**. Every section ends with
a lab task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary workbook worksheet cell cell-address cell-range formula formula-bar relative-reference absolute-reference fill-handle function autosum >}}

## 11.1 The grid: cells and ranges

A worksheet is a big grid. The **columns** have letters (A, B, C …) and the
**rows** have numbers (1, 2, 3 …). Each box is a **cell** (@fig-grid).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.1 — Cell address and range"}
The **cell address** is the column letter and the row number, for example
**B3**. A **range** is a block of cells: **B2:B4** means B2, B3 and B4.
:::

![A small sheet of the shop. B3 is selected; the range B2:B4 holds the three prices.](images/excel-grid.png){#fig-grid width=100%}

- Type in a cell and press **Enter**: the cell below is selected.
- **Text** sits on the left of a cell; **numbers** sit on the right.
- The **formula bar** above the grid shows what is really in the cell.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.1 — The shop list"}
1. Rana types *Item*, *Price (JD)* and *Quantity* in A1, B1 and C1.
2. Under them: Notebook 2 10, Pen 0.5 40, Bag 12 3.
3. The price of the pen is in **B3**; the three prices are the range
   **B2:B4**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Typing "2 JD" in a price cell. Then it is text, and Excel cannot compute
with it. Type only the number, and write "JD" in the heading.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · The shop list"}
1. Open Excel (or Excel on the web) and a new workbook.
2. Type the shop list of Example 11.1 in A1:C4.
3. Click B3. What does the Name Box (left of the formula bar) show?

*Your result:* the list, saved as `shop.xlsx`.
:::

## 11.2 Let Excel calculate: formulas

Rana wants the total of each item: price × quantity. She does not use a
calculator. She writes a **formula** (@fig-formula).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.2 — Formula"}
A **formula** starts with **=**. It uses cell addresses and the signs
**+ − * /**. The cell shows the result; the formula bar shows the formula.
:::

![D2 has =B2\*C2. The cell shows 20.](images/formula-parts.png){#fig-formula width=100%}

Excel multiplies and divides before it adds and subtracts: =2+3\*4 is 14.
Use brackets to change the order: =(2+3)\*4 is 20.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.2 — Total of the notebooks"}
1. Rana clicks D2 and types **=B2\*C2**, then presses Enter.
2. D2 shows **20** (2 × 10).
3. She changes the price in B2 to 3. D2 changes to 30 by itself.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting the =. "B2\*C2" without = is only text. Also, do not type the
numbers (=2\*10): then the total does not change when the price changes.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/formula-lab.html" poster="sims/formula-lab.png" title="Formula Lab: the Sunrise shop sheet" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · A formula"}
1. In your `shop.xlsx`, type *Total (JD)* in D1 and **=B2\*C2** in D2.
2. Change the price in B2. Watch D2.

*Your result:* D2 with the formula, and one sentence: what happened when the
price changed?
:::

## 11.3 Copy a formula: relative and absolute references

Rana needs the same formula in every row. She does not type it three times.
She **copies** it down with the **fill handle**: the small square at the
corner of the cell (@fig-refs).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.3 — Relative and absolute references"}
A **relative reference** (B2) changes when you copy the formula: in the
next row it becomes B3. An **absolute reference** has $ signs (\$F\$1) and
does **not** change when you copy.
:::

![Without $, the rate cell F1 moves to F2 and F3. With \$F\$1, it stays.](images/references.png){#fig-refs width=100%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.3 — Copying the totals"}
1. Rana selects D2 (=B2\*C2) and double-clicks the fill handle.
2. D3 gets =B3\*C3 and D4 gets =B4\*C4. Each row uses its own price and
   quantity.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.4 — One discount rate for all"}
The discount rate (10 %) is in F1. In C2 Rana writes =B2\*F1 and copies it.

1. C3 becomes =B3\*F2. F2 is empty, so the discount is 0: wrong.
2. She writes **=B2\*\$F\$1** and copies again. Now C3 is =B3\*\$F\$1: right.
3. When the rate changes to 20 %, all discounts change at once.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Forgetting the $ for a cell that every row needs (a rate, a price, a total).
Tip: after typing F1, press **F4**; Excel adds the $ signs.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/reference-lab.html" poster="sims/reference-lab.png" title="Reference Lab: copy a formula with $" height="520" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · Copy down"}
1. In `shop.xlsx`, copy D2 down to D4 with the fill handle.
2. Type 10% in F1. In E2 write =D2\*\$F\$1 and copy it down.
3. Click E4. What formula does the formula bar show?

*Your result:* columns D and E filled, and the formula of E4.
:::

## 11.4 Ready formulas: SUM, AVERAGE, MAX, MIN

Rana wants the total of the week, the average day, the best day and the
worst day. Excel has **functions** for these (@fig-functions).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 11.4 — Function"}
A **function** is a ready formula with a name, used on a range:
**=SUM(B2:B6)** adds, **=AVERAGE(B2:B6)** gives the average, **=MAX(B2:B6)**
the highest and **=MIN(B2:B6)** the lowest value.
:::

![Four functions on the sales of the week.](images/functions.png){#fig-functions width=100%}

The **AutoSum** button (Σ, Home tab) writes a SUM formula for you: click the
cell under the numbers and press Σ, then Enter.

::: {.callout-note title="Example 11.5 — The week of the shop"}
Sales: 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 JD in B2:B6.

1. =SUM(B2:B6) gives **150** JD.
2. =AVERAGE(B2:B6) gives **30** JD per day (150 ÷ 5).
3. =MAX(B2:B6) gives **50** (Thursday); =MIN(B2:B6) gives **10** (Sunday).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Error values. **#DIV/0!**: the formula divides by 0 (or by an empty cell).
**#NAME?**: a function name is wrong, for example =SUMM(B2:B6). **####**:
the column is too narrow; make it wider.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · The functions"}
1. In `shop.xlsx`, under the totals in column D, use AutoSum for the total.
2. Add the average price with =AVERAGE(B2:B4) and the highest price with
   =MAX(B2:B4).

*Your result:* `shop.xlsx` with SUM, AVERAGE and MAX.
:::

## Case study: the shop's week

Rana keeps the sales of the *Sunrise* shop in Excel. Before she presses
Enter, she wants to know what each cell will show: a total of tea
(=B2\*C2 with 3 JD and 4 packs), the sum and the average of a week of
10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 JD, the formula in D3 after she copies =B2\*C2 down,
the formula in D3 after she copies =C2\*\$F\$1 down, and a cell that divides by
an empty cell. The Game challenge of the interactive lesson uses these
cells. In the mini-game below you predict them.

{{< sim file="sims/shop-week.html" poster="sims/shop-week.png" title="The Shop's Week: what will the cell show?" kind="game" height="560" >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Lab task · The week"}
1. Type the sales of the week (Sun 10 to Thu 50) in a new sheet.
2. Add SUM, AVERAGE, MAX and MIN under them. Do the results match the
   mini-game?

*Your result:* a sheet named *Week* with the four functions.
:::

## Further reading

Microsoft Support, "Overview of formulas in Excel" and "Switch between
relative and absolute references" (support.microsoft.com). Evans, Martin
and Poatsy, *Technology in Action*, 18th ed., the chapter on productivity
software (spreadsheets).

## Exercises

1. What is in cell C4: which column and which row?
2. Write the range of the cells A2, A3, A4, A5 and A6.
3. B2 = 6 and C2 = 5. What does =B2\*C2 show?
4. What does =2+3\*4 give? And =(2+3)\*4?
5. Why must a formula start with =?
6. You copy =B2\*C2 from D2 to D5. What is in D5?
7. You copy =B2\*\$F\$1 from C2 to C4. What is in C4?
8. Sales 5, 10, 15, 20 in B2:B5. What do SUM and AVERAGE give?
9. A cell shows #NAME?. What is a likely reason?
10. What does the Σ button do?

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Column C, row 4.
2. A2:A6.
3. 30.
4. 14; 20.
5. Without =, Excel takes it as text.
6. =B5\*C5.
7. =B4\*\$F\$1.
8. SUM 50; AVERAGE 12.5.
9. A wrong function name, for example SUMM.
10. AutoSum: it writes a SUM formula for the numbers above or beside the cell.
:::
